stem: Given the mass of iron nucleus as \(55.85\,\text{u}\) and \(A = 56\), find the nuclear density?
solution:
\(m_{\text{Fe}} = 55.85,\ \text{u} = 9.27 \times 10^{-26}\,\text{kg}\)

Nuclear density \(= \dfrac{\text{mass}}{\text{volume}} = \dfrac{9.27 \times 10^{-26}}{(4\pi/3)(1.2 \times 10^{-15})^{3}} \times \dfrac{1}{56}\)

\(= 2.29 \times 10^{17}\,\text{kg m}^{-3}\)

The density of matter in neutron stars (an astrophysical object) is comparable to this density. This shows that matter in these objects has been compressed to such an extent that they resemble a big nucleus.
_note: The book prints the first solution line as "m_Fe = 55.85,  u = 9.27 x 10^-26 kg" with a stray comma between the number and the unit; it is read as m_Fe = 55.85 u = 9.27 x 10^-26 kg. Transcribed as printed.

stem: Calculate the energy equivalent of \(1\,\text{g}\) of substance.
solution:
Energy, \(E = 10^{-3} \times (3 \times 10^{8})^{2}\,\text{J}\)

\(E = 10^{-3} \times 9 \times 10^{16} = 9 \times 10^{13}\,\text{J}\)

Thus, if one gram of matter is converted to energy, there is a release of enormous amount of energy.

stem: Find the energy equivalent of one atomic mass unit, first in Joules and then in MeV. Using this, express the mass defect of \(^{16}_{8}\text{O}\) in \(\text{MeV}/c^{2}\).
solution:
\(1\,\text{u} = 1.6605 \times 10^{-27}\,\text{kg}\)

To convert it into energy units, we multiply it by \(c^{2}\) and find that

energy equivalent \(= 1.6605 \times 10^{-27} \times (2.9979 \times 10^{8})^{2}\,\text{kg m}^{2}/\text{s}^{2}\)

\(= 1.4924 \times 10^{-10}\,\text{J}\)

\(= \dfrac{1.4924 \times 10^{-10}}{1.602 \times 10^{-19}}\,\text{eV}\)

\(= 0.9315 \times 10^{9}\,\text{eV}\)

\(= 931.5\,\text{MeV}\)

or, \(1\,\text{u} = 931.5\,\text{MeV}/c^{2}\)

For \(^{16}_{8}\text{O}\), \(\Delta M = 0.13691\,\text{u} = 0.13691 \times 931.5\,\text{MeV}/c^{2} = 127.5\,\text{MeV}/c^{2}\)

The energy needed to separate \(^{16}_{8}\text{O}\) into its constituents is thus \(127.5\,\text{MeV}/c^{2}\).
_note: The book's closing sentence states the ENERGY needed to separate the nucleus as 127.5 MeV/c^2 — the unit of a mass, not an energy (the energy is 127.5 MeV). Transcribed faithfully as printed.
